1: At Jetavana in Sāvatthī, monks brought to the Buddha a young monk who had given up his effort.
2: The Buddha said, “If you give up effort on this path, you will grieve for a long time, like the Serivā tradesman who lost a golden dish,” and told a story of the past.
3: Five aeons ago in the land of Serivā, the Bodhisatta was a pedlar of pots and pans. He set out to trade with another, greedy pedlar.
4: The two crossed the river Nīlavāha by boat and entered the city of Ariṭṭhapura.
5: They divided the streets of the city between them: after one had been along a street, the other could go there later.
6: In that city was a once-rich merchant family that had fallen into poverty. Only a grandmother and her granddaughter were left, working for wages.
7: In their house lay a golden dish once used by the great merchant. Long neglected and black with tarnish, no one knew it was gold.
8: Crying out, “Pots for sale! Pots!” the greedy pedlar came to the door of that house.
9: The girl longed for an ornament, and begged her grandmother to let her trade the useless old dish for one.
10: The girl called the pedlar in, seated him, and offered him the dish, asking for anything in exchange.
11: The pedlar turned the dish over, scratched its back with a needle, and saw that it was gold.
12: Hoping to get it for nothing, he said, “It isn’t worth half a penny,” threw the dish on the floor and walked out.
13: A little later the Bodhisatta came into that street, calling out the same cry, and reached the same door.
14: The grandmother said, “The first man was rough, but this one is gentle and courteous,” and had the girl call him in.
15: As soon as the Bodhisatta took the dish, he recognised that it was gold.
16: “This dish is worth a hundred thousand. I do not have goods worth so much,” the Bodhisatta said honestly.
17: He gave them all his five hundred coins and goods worth five hundred more, asking back only his scales, his bag and eight coins.
18: The Bodhisatta hurried to the river, gave the ferryman eight coins and boarded the boat.
19: When the greedy pedlar came back and demanded the dish, the grandmother told him an honest trader had paid a thousand for it and taken it.
20: Losing his mind over his loss, he flung all his money and goods down at the door.
21: Throwing off his clothes and swinging the beam of his scales like a club, he chased the Bodhisatta to the river.
22: He shouted for the boat to turn back, but the Bodhisatta told the ferryman not to.
23: Watching the boat move away, his heart broke; he collapsed on the riverbank and died.
24: The Bodhisatta lived on, giving gifts and doing good deeds, and passed away according to his deeds.
25: When the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, that monk attained arahantship. “The foolish merchant then was Devadatta, and the wise merchant was I myself.”
